title: weave ops
description: weave-ops v1 — the WRITE side of weave's agent contract, symmetric to schema/weave-findings.schema.json. A findings document says what a merge DID; an ops document says what a caller WANTS, in the same op vocabulary over the same entity keys. Produced by `weave patch extract`, consumed by `weave patch apply`. Applying is a three-way entity merge — base = the base these ops were extracted from, ours = the target on disk, theirs = these ops replayed onto that base — so a target that has drifted is merged rather than clobbered or rejected.

schema_version.description: Semver of THIS schema. Consumers must reject a major they do not know. Additive fields are minor bumps; removing or re-meaning a field is a major bump.

file.description: Path the ops were extracted from. Its extension selects the parser; `apply` may target a different path entirely.

base.description: What the ops were computed against. Absent means the ops are anchorless: `apply` then treats the target as the base and cannot detect drift, which it reports as mode=no_base rather than hiding.

sha256.description: SHA-256 of the base content, lowercase hex. `apply` refuses a supplied base that does not hash to this — merging against the wrong ancestor produces a confidently wrong answer, which is the one outcome worth refusing.

inline.description: The base content itself. Optional and usually large; when present the document is self-contained and `apply` can run the real three-way merge with no other inputs.

exact.description: True when replaying these ops onto the declared base reproduces the changed file BYTE-FOR-BYTE at entity granularity. `weave patch extract` verifies this on itself rather than asserting it. False means entity granularity could not express the change (module-level code, reordering, an encoding change) and a whole-file fallback op is present: the round trip still holds, but applying to a drifted target degrades to a whole-file merge.

ops.description: The intent, one op per entity. Ops are keyed by the entity's name IN THE BASE, so they can still be located in a target that has not seen the change. Order is significant only in that deletions precede edits precede additions; `apply` is otherwise order-independent because every op is resolved against the ORIGINAL line indices.

op_vocabulary.description: The same alphabet as the read side. A v1 producer emits only `added | edited | renamed | rename_edited | deleted`: `unchanged` carries no intent, and the relational four (`split | merged | copied | moved`) are RESERVED — they correlate several entity keys, which a per-key matcher cannot express. A v1 consumer must accept the reserved ops without error and must not act on them.

entity.description: The key this op is about: the entity's name in the base. `(file)` on the whole-file fallback op.

entity_type.description: Parser-reported kind: function, class, method, interface, file, …

from.description: Previous name. Present for op=renamed / rename_edited.

to.description: New name. Present for op=renamed / rename_edited.

content.description: The entity's full new text, including any leading comment or decorator block that belongs to it. Absent for op=deleted.

after.description: For op=added: the entity this one follows, named as it appears IN THE BASE. Absent means the top of the file. An anchor missing from the target is not an error — the entity is appended and the op is reported as placed by fallback, because dropping an addition silently would be worse than misplacing it.

separator.description: For op=added: the whitespace or comment gap that separated this entity from its anchor, so an insertion does not weld two definitions together.

fallback.description: True on the whole-file escape hatch (entity="(file)"): weave could not express the change at entity granularity and is shipping the file. Mirrors ResolutionStrategy::Fallback on the read side — a caller reading a bare `edited` would over-trust the granularity.
